title: Why People Pay Five Figures
lede: Nobody pays twenty grand for software. They pay to stop losing more than twenty grand.
deliverable: They leave with a clear picture of why a business owner spends five figures, and a Jarvis research brief on what their chosen market is already losing.
body:
Before you pick a niche, write an offer or build a demo, you need to understand one thing: why a business owner hands over five figures. Not the tactics. The psychology. Get this and every decision after it gets easier, because you will be building an offer around something real instead of something clever.

The fear of losing beats the joy of gaining

In 1979 Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published prospect theory, the work that later won Kahneman a Nobel Prize. The finding that matters to you is simple. People do not weigh gains and losses evenly. A loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equal gain feels good. Ten thousand dollars saved is nice. Ten thousand dollars leaking out every year is a problem that has to stop.

This is why "this could save you time" gets a polite nod and nothing else. A gain is optional. A loss is not. The owner who realises they are paying a person $65k a year to do work a system could do, and have been for three years, cannot un-know that. The loss sits in front of them every day until it is fixed.

You are not creating the loss. It was always there. Everything you build in this course, the offer, the outreach, the demo, the call, exists to make a real loss visible and put a number on it.

Pain always converts to money

Owners describe pain in all sorts of currencies. Time. Stress. Staff. Missed calls. Slow jobs. None of those are the unit anyone buys in. Every one of them converts to dollars, and the conversion is what turns "that's annoying" into "that has to stop".

The pain as they feel itWhat it actually is
"It takes ages."Hours per week, times the hourly cost of whoever does it, times 48 weeks.
"We have someone who handles that."That person's wage, or the share of it spent on work a system could do.
"The software does most of it."The subscription, plus per job or per user fees, plus the support tickets nobody counts.
"We miss a few calls."Calls missed per week, times the close rate, times the average job value.
"Jobs take longer than they should."Extra jobs they could complete per month if the bottleneck was gone, times margin.

If it is efficiency, you are making their money better spent. If it is staff, overhead is cash. If it is capacity, it is revenue they are turning away. Everything comes back to money. The owner who has never added it up is the one who pays you to make it stop.

An illustrative example. A mid sized construction company runs its jobs through a generic CRM. The platform costs around $13k a year, and the old invoicing tool charged $100 per customer account on top. An office administrator works three days a week, mostly on tasks the CRM cannot do automatically: chasing sign offs, re-entering quotes, sending reminders. She costs over $65k a year. Jobs take several weeks start to finish, and in busy months they turn work away.

Ask the owner how things are going and you get "we've got a CRM and an admin, it works fine". Add it up and the same business is paying roughly $78k a year for a system that still needs a human to babysit it, and leaving jobs on the table every week. Nothing about the business changed between those two sentences. Only the maths did. The numbers are the kind Blake has seen in real deals and are here to show the conversion, not as a client result.

Price lives inside the size of the problem

Once the loss has a number, price stops being about you. If a problem costs a business $2k a year and you try to charge $20k to solve it, there is a disconnect no sales skill fixes. Flip it. If the problem costs them $5 million a year, $50k for a website is a sensible decision, assuming the solution genuinely solves it. To them it is not a cost. It is an investment that pays back many times over.

The Australian government spent $96 million on a website. Yes, government contracts are bloated. Yes, it is an extreme example. But it happened because the budget existed and the problem was worth that much to them. Price always lives inside the size of the problem.

So the question is never "what is my AI worth?" The question is "what is this market losing, and what fraction of that is an obvious yes?" A small slice of a real, quantified problem is an easy yes. A big slice of a vague one is impossible. How that becomes an actual price on an actual call is Module 6. For now, hold the principle.

What this means for the offer you are about to build

You are not looking for businesses that might like AI. You are looking for a market where the same loss repeats business after business, big enough to be worth five figures to stop, and visible enough that you can point at it. That is the whole brief for the next two lessons and for the strategy session: find the repeated loss first, build the offer around it second.

What Jarvis does here

Jarvis can do the first pass of this research for you. Give it a market you are considering and it will map where that market is losing money, in dollars, so you walk into the next lesson with a shortlist of real losses instead of a guess.

I am researching a market I may build an AI service for: [describe the market, for example residential builders with five to twenty staff in Australia]. Research how businesses in this market typically lose money through manual work, missed enquiries, slow processes, staff doing repeatable admin, or software that does not fit. For each loss, estimate the annual dollar cost for a typical business using these rules: hours become hourly cost times 48 weeks, staff become wage share on removable work, software becomes subscription plus per use fees, missed enquiries become missed calls times close rate times average job value, slow jobs become extra jobs per month times margin. Show assumptions in a table, mark every number you estimated, cite where the public evidence came from, and rank the losses from largest to smallest. Finish with the three losses most likely to be worth five figures to stop, and the question I would ask an owner to confirm each one.

Do this now

Run that prompt on the market you are leaning towards. If you have no market yet, run it on two you are curious about. Read the ranked losses and write one sentence in your own words: "Businesses in [market] lose roughly [number] a year to [loss]." That sentence is the seed of your offer. If you cannot write it with a dollar figure in it, the market is not ready, or the research is not done.

Bring that sentence and the Jarvis research to your weekly group strategy session. It is where we start, because the offer, the outreach and the demo all get built on top of it.
